Two practical cautions carry into collection: the Czech word 'akvizice' means M&A, not acquiring, so queries must use 'akceptace/přijímání platebních karet' or the bare loanword 'acquiring'; and the Global Payments Czech properties (globalpayments.cz, gpwebpay.cz) serve HTTP 403 to scripted fetches and need a real browser fingerprint rather than being written off as dead.

Czech online payment acceptance is served by a dense, consolidating layer of payment institutions whose public footprint splits sharply in two: a marketing layer (press rooms, blogs, merchant case studies) that is rich in merchant wins and product roadmap but poor in hard numbers, and a statutory layer (ČNB JERRS licences, Sbírka listin annual reports) that is authoritative but slow. The strongest direct sources are Comgate's Pro média page — unusually publishing both dated tiskové zprávy and 2020-2024 annual reports — GoPay's tiskové zprávy archive (18k e-shops, a stated CZK 90bn 2025 volume target, now inside Worldline), PayU's Czech-language Zprávy a média, and GP webpay, a major gateway absent from the seed list and found only by snowballing. Coverage is uneven at the edges: ThePay publishes nothing at all and is reachable only through its IČO 28135261 filings, Adyen and Stripe have no Czech local press room despite the cell brief assuming one, and Revolut's newsroom is bot-defended (403, presumed live). Two headline expectations for this cell did not survive contact with the evidence — instant-payment adoption and payment-method mix are not published by the gateways themselves and must be sourced from ČNB statistics and APEK research instead, so this cell is best treated as a merchant-win, ownership and product-rail sensor rather than a payments-volume data source.

The Czech consumer-credit/BNPL/wallet cell splits cleanly into three publishing layers. The specialists — Twisto (now owned by Turkey's Param), ČSOB's Skip Pay, PPF's Home Credit a.s., KB/Société Générale's ESSOX, Cofidis CZ, and the previously unlisted bank-owned arms PlatímPak (Raiffeisenbank) and Inbank CZ — are prolific, dated press publishers with quantitative nuggets (Skip Pay's 99% on-time repayment claim, ESSOX's contract and unit volumes, Home Credit's May 2026 exit from short-term lending), but not one of them publishes financial statements on its own site. That financial layer therefore lives entirely in the Sbírka listin at justice.cz and in foreign parent disclosures (PPF, Home Credit Group, KBC/ČSOB, Inbank Group), while ČNB's JERRS register is the authoritative and machine-readable spine for licence status and for discovering the long tail of licensed providers. The richest and most differentiated finding is the merchant-integration layer that the cell rationale anticipated: the Shoptet addon catalogue enumerates the full competitive set of Czech checkout BNPL providers in one place, Skip Pay's developer portal names its gateway and SaaS-platform partners explicitly, Twisto's docs mark which integration paths are deprecated, and Twisto and PlatímPak both publish browsable partner e-shop directories that can be diffed into an adoption time series. The main caveat on this pass is methodological: the session's search budget was exhausted before the cell began, so everything here came from direct fetching and link-snowballing, which biases the map toward well-resourced incumbents and leaves the smaller lenders, foreign entrants and the wallet sub-sector thinly covered.

The Czech scheme-and-rails layer splits cleanly into three publisher types. First, the ČNB is an unusually generous operator-of-record: CERTIS gets its own portal with a rulebook, versioned participant lists in CSV, a monthly statistics series exposed through ARAD set D458, a dedicated instant-payments page carrying adoption share and the 2027 euro-instant deadlines, the proxy-lookup Registr pro platby na kontakt, and — new since June 2026 — a National Payments Forum whose instant-payments and fraud working groups should become the earliest forward signal in this cell. Second, the card schemes publish only marketing-grade Czech press releases and no CZ-level financials, and Mastercard's Czech estate is 403-blocked to automated fetching while Visa's Czech newsroom hides behind an English URL path; the practical workaround for both is the Sdružení pro bankovní karty estate (bankovnikarty.cz / cardmag.cz), a legacy windows-1250 static site that quietly holds the only long-run scheme-neutral CZ card dataset (quarterly XLSX back to 2000, history to 1989) plus a 531-file archive of Visa and Mastercard press releases running to August 2026. Third, Bank iD is well covered for news and adoption factsheets but publishes no annual report, so its ownership and economics are reachable only through the statutory Sbírka listin under IČO 09513817. The binding constraint on this slice is tooling, not sources: the session's search budget was exhausted before any query ran, so everything here was found by direct fetch and snowballing, and three critical targets (mastercard.cz, the EPC document library, ARAD) will need a headless browser before they can be collected at all.

Czech ATM and cash-handling intelligence rests on a narrow but high-quality base: Euronet is the only independent deployer of scale found (self-reporting ~10% of a ~5,000-machine national estate, ~300 of ~1,200 ATMs in Prague), while cash-in-transit is effectively a Loomis/Brink's duopoly, with the fate of G4S's Czech cash business unresolved. Because all three Czech operating entities are private subsidiaries with no local investor relations, their only recurring hard disclosure is the statutory účetní závěrka/výroční zpráva filed into the court Sbírka listin (confirmed live for IČO 25608452 and 26110709), backstopped by ARES for entity resolution and by parent-level reporting at Euronet Worldwide, Loomis AB and Brink's. Public-sector channels — Věstník veřejných zakázek, NEN and Registr smluv — are the only route to actual cash-logistics contract terms and pricing, since bank–operator agreements are disclosed by neither side. The critical structural weakness is fleet attribution: ČNB counts only 'bankomaty provozované českými bankami' (4.9k at end-2025, with withdrawals down to 140.4m transactions) and the SBK whole-estate series died around 2011, so the bank-owned versus deployer-owned split has no authoritative publisher and must be derived from ČNB anchors plus OSM/directory operator tagging.

Czech bank-technology vendors function exactly as the cell rationale predicts: with the systemic banks private and their procurement invisible, the supplier's own case-study library is the public record, and four vendors carry almost all of it — Profinit (named projects at Komercni banka, Ceska sporitelna, Raiffeisenbank, Equa Bank and Erste Group), Trask (J&T Bank, MONETA, Raiffeisenbank, Ceska sporitelna, plus the Impresto lending and Verification-of-Payee lines), Adastra (Tatra banka, Raiffeisenbank and card-transaction categorisation, mirrored in Czech at /cs/success-stories/) and Monet+ (CSOB, Ceska sporitelna and Air Bank on digital identity and card acceptance). Aricoma discloses relationships rather than projects — its customer wall names CSOB Group, Ceska sporitelna, Raiffeisenbank, ING and Citibank while its newsroom is M&A-dominated — and ICZ contributes the rare state-owned-bank artefact in CEBIS for Ceska exportni banka. Three structural cautions shape collection: Cleverlance now redirects to Avenga rather than Aricoma, so a whole delivery organisation sits outside the cell as briefed; CCA Group publishes no banking references at all; and Unicorn, GEM System and Asseco Central Europe are silent, loop-blocked and 403-blocked respectively, the latter two being client-side limitations rather than dead sources. Because vendor claims are self-reported marketing, the cell should be anchored on three neutral spines — Registr smluv and Hlidac statu's free API for contracts, NEN for public procurement, and the Sbirka listin for the audited accounts that are the only financial disclosure these privately held vendors ever make — with SystemOnLine's banking vertical and vendor directory as the snowball engine for the actors the seed list missed.

For Czech references, this cell's source landscape is sharply uneven: Temenos is the one global vendor with a verified, well-structured Czech trail — Komerční banka selection and go-live press releases plus a success story, all English-only, all reachable through a newsroom with Region/Category/Year filters and a working on-site search — while Diebold Nixdorf's and NCR Atleos's public case-study libraries carry no Czech customer at all, which is itself the competitor-positioning evidence the cell was created to produce. The best-automatable endpoints are NCR Atleos's investor RSS, Auriga's feed and ATM Marketplace's feed, but the Atleos archive is at real risk from the pending Brink's acquisition and should be mirrored now; a further six central sources (Finastra, Printec, Asseco CE, Finextra, Fiserv, SEC EDGAR) returned 403s or timeouts that read as bot defences rather than dead links, so this cell needs a headless-browser collector and a declaring User-Agent for SEC before it goes live. Local-language reality is that no global vendor in this cell runs a Czech-language site — the Diebold Nixdorf cs-cz path 500s, comarch.cz is parked, printec.cz fails TLS — so Czech-language pickup has to be caught downstream at ČTK's Protext wire and in the Czech trade press (Bankovnictví online, IT Systems/SystemOnLine), all three verified live. The whole slice was produced without a single search-engine query because the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted and every fallback engine blocked or cache-collided, so treat it as high-precision, deliberately incomplete on recall, and worth re-running against a live index.

All six seeded Czech sector associations were located and mapped, and the cell divides cleanly into two tiers. The high-value tier is ČBA (member roster of ~33 banks plus the separate ČBA Monitor statistics property carrying sector aggregates, the Hypomonitor mortgage series and the ČBA Prognóza), SBK (quarterly and annual card statistics spanning 2001-2026, plus a named contributor roster of 27 issuers and acquirers and a dated log of market exits that doubles as the best enumeration of non-bank Czech payments actors found anywhere in this cell), APEK (570 enumerable members across 64 static pages, plus the APEKdata portal with a dedicated online-payments section), and ČLFA (current quarterly leasing, consumer-credit and factoring statistics, an active press stream, and hosting for the otherwise-invisible Asociace factoringových společností ČR series). AKAT contributes a codified fund-data programme and quarterly aggregates including DIP uptake, while ČEFTAS is the weakest of the six as a data source — its official press category has been dormant since May 2022, though its article stream is current. Snowballing extended the cell to AČSS (building societies) and ČASF (advisory and intermediation distribution), and surfaced the SBK-adjacent trade press and conference circuit as a people-and-vendor index; ČAP remains unverified behind an apparent bot defence. Two collection caveats dominate: three of the six member rosters (ČLFA, ČEFTAS, AKAT) require headless-browser rendering, and ČBA is both JS-rendered — recoverable only through its 2,838-URL sitemap — and has its annual-report PDF store placed off-limits by robots.txt.

Czech financial announcements run on two rails, and the wire is the stronger one: ČTK's Protext service (protext.cz, mirrored at ceskenoviny.cz/pr/ and, per the operator, 27 further portals) carries banks, the banking association, card schemes' partners and small payment firms alike, with a date/language/origin search over roughly 50,525 records and a finance-and-economics category running to about 440 pages — a single crawlable archive that persists after company pages change and that captures actors with no newsroom at all. Corporate newsrooms are the second rail and are markedly less tractable: paths drift far from the obvious /o-nas/pro-media template ('pro novináře' at Air Bank, 'servis pro média' at MONETA, 'informační servis' at Raiffeisenbank, an off-domain host at mBank CZ), listings are frequently client-rendered, RSS is almost absent outside ČNB, and ČSOB, UniCredit CZ and CREDITAS all refused automated fetches while remaining evidently live. Around these sit the retrospective archives and intermediaries — NEWTON Media (from 1989), Anopress and Monitora, plus the APRA and Mediář agency indexes — which are licensable rather than crawlable but reach back further than the free web. The main caveat on this slice is method: the session's web-search budget was exhausted before the first query, so everything here came from direct fetches and link-snowballing in Czech, and the long tail of small payment institutions and fintechs that a cs-language search sweep would surface remains unmapped.

Czech mainstream business media form a compact, highly concentrated landscape dominated by four publishing houses — Economia (Hospodářské noviny, Ekonom, Aktuálně.cz), Czech News Center (E15), MAFRA (iDNES, Lidovky) and Seznam.cz (Seznam Zprávy, Novinky.cz) — sitting on top of one wire, ČTK, whose ČeskéNoviny.cz and Protext PR service timestamp and seed most bank-results coverage before any outlet adds interpretation. Only E15 maintains an explicit banking beat ('Finance a bankovnictví'); everywhere else banking sits inside a general Ekonomika/Byznys rubric, so downstream Czech-language keyword and entity filtering is unavoidable. The analytically richest material — executive comment, deal detail, unpublished figures — is concentrated behind paywalls (Ekonom hard-walled, HN+, Deník N, e15 Premium) and in print, which makes a licensed aggregator (Newton Media/NewtonOne, possibly Monitora or Anopress) or a small set of publisher subscriptions a prerequisite rather than an optimisation; free, RSS-friendly coverage from Aktuálně.cz, Seznam Zprávy, ČT24 and ČTK gives good breadth and speed but mostly wire-level depth. This slice was built entirely by direct fetching and navigation snowballing because the session's search budget was exhausted before it started, so section URLs here are structurally verified but long-tail discovery, the journalist/newsletter/podcast layers, and the two blocked MAFRA titles remain open and should be closed on a re-run.

Every systemic Czech bank in scope reports upward into a foreign parent, and the parent's investor-reporting stack is a genuinely separate channel: English-language, quarter-driven, and substantially richer on Czech volumes, market shares, cost/income and digital plans than the local entity's own disclosure. The densest sources are Erste Group (Czech Republic geographic segment plus an XLSX data-sheet workbook), KBC (a dedicated 'Czech Republic Business Unit' chapter in every quarterly report, on a stable CDN URL pattern), and RBI (Central Europe segment, XLSM data, and a one-page group-authored Czech country sheet); SG and UniCredit are thinner and require mining Excel supplements, URD country-by-country annexes and CEE decks, while PPF is unlisted and discloses through consolidated annual accounts, sub-holding reports and arranger-hosted bond prospectuses. Payments extends the cell usefully — Worldline (KB SmartPay), Euronet and Global Payments all disclose Czech acquiring, ATM and processing detail at group level, with the US filers giving the most granular and most machine-readable archive. The principal constraints are that almost none of this exists in Czech (only subsidiary press-room relays, Czech-law prospectuses and pse.cz issuer pages do), and that most numbers sit inside PDFs, so collection should key on the structured artefacts first and treat the OeKB-style statutory archives as the durable completeness backstop.

The Czech specialist retail-finance media layer is dense, mature and unusually machine-friendly: Mesec.cz is the anchor, publishing a dated, sortable per-bank fee table (~30+ current accounts, with monthly maintenance 0-490 Kc, own/partner ATM withdrawal and counter-withdrawal lines, stamped 'updated 1. 7. 2026') alongside a confirmed RSS feed, with Finparada.cz, Finance.cz and Banky.cz providing three further independent normalisations of the same underlying sazebniky - which is what makes cross-checking, and therefore change detection, viable. The professional tier is real but gated: Bankovnictvi (bankovnictvionline.cz, publisher 4H production s.r.o.) is actively running named executive interviews (KBC, Komercni banka, CSOB, CNB, EY) plus /technologie, /regulace and a /personalie appointments feed behind a subscription, and is complemented on the distribution side by PROFI Poradenstvi & Finance and the Poradci-sobe.cz adviser community, and on the vendor side by IT Systems' 'Banky a financni organizace' vertical. Award and catalogue properties - Zlata koruna (700+ products, results 2009-2025) and Banka roku (24 editions) - offer ready-made longitudinal panels of Czech bank product posture that are entirely external to bank self-disclosure. Two hard caveats on this slice: WebSearch was exhausted before a single seed query could run, so discovery was by URL hypothesis and snowballing only and is biased toward guessable names; and Penize.cz plus its sister Finmag - one of the two portals this cell is named for - returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, which reads as bot defence rather than death and must be re-attempted with a browser-grade client before any completeness claim is made.

Czech fintech and payments weak signals concentrate in a small number of Prague-based outlets, and Lupa.cz is the clear anchor: it maintains genuine, actively-updated Czech-language topic archives at /n/fintech/ (101 articles), /n/platby/ (127) and /n/bankovnictvi/ (34), plus a verified RSS 2.0 feed, making it the cheapest high-yield ingestion point in this cell. CzechCrunch has the greater reach and the faster wire — its timestamped /live/ feed carries fintech launch and partnership items several times a day — but it exposes no fintech tag archive, so it must be worked through section indexes and on-site search instead. Around that core sit the Czech Fintech Association (an 80+ member directory and a 200+ firm export brochure, the best actor-map pointers found), the trade title Časopis Bankovnictví with its distinctive /personalie/ executive-move feed, the state CzechStartups.gov.cz directories, and English-language regional coverage via Tech.eu and The Recursive. Two caveats bound this slice hard: WebSearch was exhausted before the first query, so nothing was found by search engine and the long tail of independent Czech fintech blogs, newsletters and podcasts remains undiscovered; and six targets including the cell-named Forbes.cz could not be read (JS rendering or HTTP 403) and are recorded as unverified hypotheses, not as dead.

The Czech interpretation-and-archive layer over bank disclosures rests on two solid pillars and one broken one. Patria Online is the strongest: its research hub was confirmed carrying live Czech-language recommendations and target prices for all three listed banks (Komerční banka, Moneta, Erste), with per-issuer consensus, news and financials tabs and an explicit Czech earnings calendar — making it the anchor source for this cell. Akcie.cz (Fio-affiliated) supplies a genuinely independent second broker view with dated target-price notes and sequential article IDs that make historical backfill cheap, while Kurzy.cz contributes an 'Oficiální sdělení' and 'Tiskové zprávy' archive that mirrors issuer announcements beyond the life of the original pages; Roklen24, by contrast, has narrowed to FX commentary and no longer belongs at seed weight. The broken pillar is ratings: Moody's and S&P both returned 403 and Fitch was blocked outright, so the highest-credibility layer is present in the map but not yet collectible, and ESMA's free European Rating Platform — the obvious licence-clean substitute — could not be located. Two structural caveats bound this slice: WebSearch was unavailable for its entire duration, so no cs- or en-language query discovery ran, and analyst coverage exists only for the three listed banks, leaving ČSOB, Raiffeisenbank CZ and UniCredit CZ reachable through rating actions and parent-group research alone.

The English-language layer over Czech banking and payments splits into four tiers: authoritative international wires (Reuters, Bloomberg, plus CTK's licensed English service upstream of both) that carry Czech bank results, M&A and licence events but are paywalled, bot-defended and unscrapable; a CEE regional tier (bne IntelliNews, which explicitly desks the Czech Republic, and Emerging Europe, whose on-site search returned genuine Czech banking and fintech articles) that is the most collectible high-signal layer; a payments and banking-technology trade tier (Finextra - the only outlet here publishing a confirmed RSS feed - plus The Paypers, Retail Banker International, Central Banking for CNB matters, and FinTech Futures) where Czech items appear as vendor deals and regulatory notes; and a local English-for-expats tier (Expats.cz Business & Money at /czech-news/economy, Prague Morning, Radio Prague International) that functions as the de facto translation channel for consumer-facing Czech banking news. Two structural cautions: the large global payments outlets treat Czechia as incidental (a PYMNTS search for 'Czech' surfaced no Czech-focused headline on page one), and one former fit for this cell, Kafkadesk, has been repurposed into unrelated affiliate content. The material limitation of this run is that the session's web-search budget was fully consumed before this agent's first query, so all discovery was done by direct fetching and on-site snowballing and the mandatory Czech-language leg was never executed - this cell should be re-run with search available before its coverage is considered complete.

The Czech statutory quarterly disclosure set is one of the best-organised source cells in the region because the regulator itself maintains the index: ČNB publishes six 'Přehled odkazů na webové stránky…' pages mapping every bank, third-country branch, credit union, financial holding, investment company, pension company and securities dealer to the URL of its own disclosure corner — 24 banks and 6 credit unions were enumerated with deep links from this slice alone, covering unlisted institutions (Fio, Air Bank, CREDITAS, Trinity, PPF banka, Partners Banka, Artesa, NEY, Citfin) whose quarterly XLSX files are their only structured public financial reporting, including ownership, organisational chart, branch counts and FTE headcount. The decisive finding is that the legal compulsion has lapsed: Part Five and Annexes 10/13 of Decree 163/2014 Sb. were repealed with effect from 1.7.2025 and prudential disclosure is migrating to the EBA's centralised Pillar 3 Data Hub, so the cell is now a voluntary-continuation regime — empirically still running (MONETA, PPF banka, Fio, ČEB, Citfin, Artesa and RSTS all published into 2026) but no longer guaranteed uniform, and the historical archive should be mirrored now. Practical collection is harder than the tidy index suggests: about a third of the regulator's own deep links are stale after site migrations, rebrands and mergers (PPF banka and ČEB 404, ČMSS/Buřinka/RSTS/MONETA redirect, Modrá pyramida now serves a kb.cz certificate, Max banka ceased to exist on 1.10.2024 with its series frozen at Q3 2024), and seven of the largest names — ČSOB, ČSOB Hypoteční banka, UniCredit, CREDITAS, ČSOB Stavební spořitelna, plus JS-rendered Česká spořitelna and Air Bank — cannot be harvested without a real-browser tier. Terminology is the other trap: the template is standardized but its label is not, alternating across 'povinně uveřejňované' and 'povinně zveřejňované informace', 'povinné údaje o bance', 'informace o bance', 'údaje uveřejňované čtvrtletně', 'informace dle vyhlášky ČNB', 'veřejné informace' and plain 'dokumenty ke stažení', so any rediscovery pass must run the full variant set rather than a single Czech phrase.

The Prague issuer channel is a three-layer stack rather than one website: BCPP's live surfaces on pse.cz (per-ISIN issuer pages, the /novinky announcement search, the corporate event calendar, and the four segment rosters), an undocumented but largely open bulk server at ftp.pse.cz holding the exchange's own copies of issuer annual and half-year reports (including ESEF XHTML) alongside index and statistics files, and the ČNB Centrální úložiště regulovaných informací (OAM) which is the statutory, regulator-timestamped repository and the real authority when an IR page is later edited or withdrawn. For banking and payments the important correction is that the equity channel is thin — only Komerční banka, Moneta Money Bank and Erste Group Bank on Prime, SAB Finance on Standard, and Eurowag/WAG Payment plus foreign banks on the Free Market, with no fintech at all on START at scan time — while the debt-securities lists are dense with Czech banks (Moneta, Raiffeisenbank, UniCredit Bank CZ, J&T Banka, J&T Finance Group) that carry exchange disclosure duty through mortgage-covered and perpetual bond listings without any listed equity. The main obstacles are technical rather than legal: the announcement and calendar surfaces render client-side with no RSS or documented API, the Burzovní věstník and issuer master-data branches of the ftp server are 401-gated, and the filing archives are keyed by abbreviated exchange codes that still need resolving to ISINs; a publicly indexed staging host, tst22.pse.cz, should be explicitly blocklisted so it never contaminates provenance.

For Czech banking and payments, the Czech National Bank is not one source but a small federation of disclosure infrastructure, and it is the correct starting index for the entire landscape. Three OAM-family applications on oam.cnb.cz carry the filed content — the centrální úložiště regulovaných informací (annual and half-yearly reports, inside information, managers' transactions, major-holdings notifications, plus a pre-2009 archive), the registr prospektů and the registr konečných podmínek základních prospektů, and the short-positions register — while JERRS on jerrs.cnb.cz is the authoritative roster of every licensed bank, payment institution, e-money institution and small-scale payment service provider, exposed as HTML, as seven open-data CSV/JSON datasets, and as a certificate-gated SOAP API (WS JERRS). The decisive asymmetry for this run is that the frictionless bulk feeds cover the banking and credit-intermediation side only: the payments categories have no open dataset and must be reached by scraping JERRS, by the ČNB PSRI statistical list, or via the EBA PSD2 register, and the OAM itself has no export at all until ESAP arrives in 2027. Because most CZ banks and payment institutions are not listed issuers and never appear in OAM, the IČO exposed by every ČNB register is the load-bearing join key into the sbírka listin at or.justice.cz, which is where their annual reports actually live.

For Czech banking and payments, the statutory disclosure floor is the Ministry of Justice public register and its Sbírka listin: every Czech-incorporated bank, payment institution, processor, ATM operator and IT supplier must lodge účetní závěrka, výroční zpráva, zpráva auditora and (in groups) zpráva o vztazích there, free to read, which makes it the only channel where a silent private payments company still reveals revenue, auditor and intra-group relations — confirmed live on a bank with an unbroken 2018-2024 series. The practical architecture is two-layer: ARES (open REST API, IČO/NACE/legal form) and the ISVR bulk open data build and refresh the actor universe, then per-entity or.justice.cz URLs (rejstrik-$firma?ico= -> vypis-sl-firma?subjektId= -> vypis-sl-detail?dokument=) fetch the actual filings, with úplný výpis supplying name changes, shareholders and branches that no company website lists. The binding constraints are legal and mechanical rather than editorial: the register web UI is capped at 3000 requests/day and 50/minute with random CAPTCHA, the ISVR open-data licence states non-commercial use and GDPR controller status, there is no bulk feed of the deed PDFs (which are Czech-only and often scanned), and the beneficial-ownership register ESM was closed to the public on 17 December 2025 — so ownership depth now needs a lawful access route or a commercial provider (CRIBIS, Dun & Bradstreet CZ, Merk). Priorities: enumerate the actor list from ČNB's licensed-entity register plus NACE sweeps in ARES, settle the ISVR licence question, and build the OCR/extraction stage before scaling collection.

The Czech debt-investor disclosure channel has an unusually clean spine: ČNB publishes the closed list of six banks licensed to run a covered block (UniCredit Bank CZ&SK, Česká spořitelna, Hypoteční banka, MONETA Money Bank, Raiffeisenbank and Komerční banka) with LEI/IČO and the ISINs entitled to the 'European Covered Bond (Premium)' label, and runs two Oracle-based registers — approved prospectuses and final terms/emisní dodatky — that together date-stamp essentially every bank bond programme and tranche in the country, plus an OAM store that captures regulated filings from debt-only issuers invisible to equity IR. The rich data, though, lives on the issuer side and is uneven: Komerční banka and MONETA publish exemplary debt pages (quarterly Covered Bond Investor Reports, machine-readable HTT workbooks, cover-pool overviews, full AT1/T2/SNP prospectus stacks), Česká spořitelna began HTT reporting in 2026 on a CZK 308.5bn cover pool, UniCredit CZ&SK runs the largest labelled XS franchise behind a 403-guarded site, while Raiffeisenbank and Hypoteční banka hold licensed cover pools with no cover-pool disclosure surface located at all. Terminology is the main recall risk — three coexisting Czech renderings (hypoteční zástavní listy, kryté dluhopisy/krytý blok, evropský krytý dluhopis) and no native term for senior non-preferred — and four issuer hosts (UniCredit, ČSOB, ČSOB Hypoteční banka, CREDITAS) returned 403/500 to plain fetches while their PDFs remain reachable, so a headless-browser tier is a prerequisite rather than an optimisation. Pan-European scaffolding (Covered Bond Label HTT database, ECBC Fact Book, free NORD/LB Floor Research) fills the interpretive layer and is the fastest way to detect a new Czech filing.

The Czech non-bank licensed segment is unusually well mapped by its own regulator: ČNB maintains five parallel 'přehled odkazů' index pages that deep-link each licensed entity to its own statutory disclosure page, and between them they define this cell's entire universe — 5 building societies (ČSOB Stavební spořitelna, Modrá pyramida, MONETA, Raiffeisen, Buřinka), 6 credit unions, 9 pension companies, 8 investment companies and 35 investment firms — with JERRS and the Sbírka listin as authoritative backstops. Disclosure quality is highly uneven: Raiffeisen and MONETA publish bilingual annual reports on disciplined schedules and Artesa publishes parseable quarterly XLSX, while the smaller credit unions and several bank-group managers require commercial-register retrieval, and English-language coverage is close to absent outside those two building societies. The cell's distinctive payoff is already visible — Modrá pyramida's ~190 branches converting to KB advisory points with ~500 advisors absorbed and servicing migrating to KB+, and Patria Finance describing its own trading-platform development — none of which is broken out in the parent groups' consolidated reports. The main risks to collection are stale regulator links after rebrands (cmss.cz), TLS/host mismatches on entities mid-integration (modrapyramida.cz), and archive loss during the several site migrations now under way.

The Czech public-sector financial landscape in this cell is unusually well documented but almost entirely PDF-based and Czech-first: NRB, ČEB, EGAP, GSFT, the CNB, the Financial Arbiter and MF all maintain deep, stable annual-report archives (EGAP 2003-2025, GSFT 2005-2025 on predictable paths, ČEB 2012-2025, NRB 2002-2025, CNB with a genuine English mirror), and MF adds a near-monthly state-ownership register that makes the ownership chain over EGAP and the ČEB/NRB group traceable in near-real time. Because these bodies publish on a public-accountability rather than investor basis, three routes exist that commercial-bank cells do not have: statutory reporting to the Chamber of Deputies (EGAP and CNB submissions, findable via fulltext.psp.cz), independent NKÚ audit conclusions that have historically contradicted the institutions' own accounts, and full procurement exposure through E-ZAK/NEN/TenderArena plus the Registr smluv, which names IT and services suppliers and contract values outright. The main risks to a collection plan are structural rather than technical: ČEB is being absorbed into NRB under the 2024 National Development Bank Act, so reporting perimeters and time series will break; the same statutory duty appears under two near-identical Czech slugs (povinně uveřejňované vs. zveřejňované), and MF content straddles mfcr.cz and mf.gov.cz. No first-party API exists for any core entity, so machine-readable collection must lean on Hlídač státu, MONITOR státní pokladna and the Registr smluv, with EGAP's tokenised download links re-scraped rather than cached.
